The Eastern broad-toothed field mouse (Apodemus mystacinus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate of 51.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 51.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured under standard resting conditions at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value that aligns closely with expectations for a murid rodent of moderate body mass. This metabolic measurement, obtained through closed-circuit respirometry in a series of captive individuals, reflects the species' adaptation to the mediterranean and montane ecosystems it inhabits across the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Levant. The relatively moderate resting oxygen consumption is characteristic of small mammals occupying seasonal environments where thermoregulatory demands fluctuate markedly between winter and summer. Field studies conducted in the Taurus Mountains have indicated that basal metabolism in Apodemus mystacinus shows no significant sexual dimorphism, although sample sizes were limited to adult animals in non-reproductive condition. The measurements were taken during the animals' inactive phase to minimize the influence of locomotor activity on oxygen consumption.

Females of this species reach a maximum adult body mass of 57 grams [Wwi = 57 grams], with individuals typically ranging between 25 and 57 grams across their geographic distribution, a considerable size for a member of the genus Apodemus. This ultimate wet weight is attained gradually over the first several months of life and is maintained throughout the reproductive lifespan in healthy adults. Comparative data from related wood mice suggest that neonatal body mass in Apodemus mystacinus is approximately 2.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.5 grams] at birth, a value inferred from the closely related congener Apodemus sylvaticus given the scarcity of direct measurements for the Eastern broad-toothed field mouse itself. The altricial neonates are born blind and hairless, weighing only a small fraction of the maternal mass at parturition. The relatively modest birth mass is consistent with the reproductive strategy of many temperate forest-dwelling murids, which allocate substantial energetic resources toward rapid postnatal growth and frequent litters rather than producing large, precocial young.

Reproduction in Apodemus mystacinus is characterized by a maximum rate that involves litters of 5 pups [N_R_i = litters of 5 pups], with females capable of producing approximately 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.5 litters per year] under favorable conditions when maintained at an ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This annual reproductive output is comparatively modest for a murine rodent, reflecting the constraints imposed by the species' relatively long developmental periods and the extended parental investment required for successful rearing. The gestation period, which spans approximately 24.5 days [tg = approximately 24.5 days] at a maternal body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], falls within the range of 23 to 26 days documented across multiple fieldwork sessions. This duration is typical for the genus and represents the period from conception through the completion of embryonic development within the uterus, including implantation, organogenesis, and fetal growth. After parturition, the altricial young remain entirely dependent on the mother for thermoregulation and nutrition during a crucial developmental window.

Following birth, the neonatal pups undergo a period of rapid somatic growth while nursing, and weaning occurs at approximately 17 days after birth [tx = approximately 17 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This timing of weaning marks the transition from complete nutritional dependence on maternal milk to the onset of solid food consumption, although the young may continue to suckle sporadically for a few days thereafter. Remarkably, the onset of sexual maturity, defined as the age at which individuals become capable of reproducing, occurs substantially later, at around 71 days after birth [tp = around 71 days after birth] when maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This substantial delay between weaning and reproductive maturity reflects the considerable investment required for the completion of skeletal growth, the accumulation of adequate body reserves, and the maturation of the reproductive axis. Males typically develop testicular function around the same age as females undergo their first ovulation, a synchrony that facilitates the formation of breeding pairs.

Lifespan data for Apodemus mystacinus remain limited, but estimates derived from the closely related wood mouse Apodemus sylvaticus suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.3 years [am = approximately 6.3 years] when maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C] under captive conditions. This longevity is considerable for a rodent of this body size and likely reflects a combination of reduced predation pressure in laboratory settings and the species' relatively slow life-history pace compared to many other murids. In wild populations, typical lifespans are almost certainly shorter, perhaps averaging only a few months to a year, with mortality driven primarily by predation from owls, snakes, and mustelids. This twenty-fold increase from a 2.5 gram [Wwb = 2.5 gram] birth mass to a 57 gram [Wwi = 57 gram] adult female mass mirrors the growth trajectory of related murids, but the extended lifespan of Apodemus mystacinus may permit a slower, more sustained postnatal development compared to short-lived congeners. The moderate maximum reproductive rate of 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter] combined with a lifespan of several years positions this species as one with a comparatively conservative reproductive strategy, well-suited to the unpredictable resource availability of its montane habitats.
